The Chan Master Huaihai of Baizhang Mountain in Hongzhou was a native of Changle in Fuzhou.
While the Master was attending upon Mazu as they were walking along, they saw a flock of wild ducks fly past. Mazu asked, "What is that? The Master replied, "Wild ducks.
Mazu asked, "Where have they gone? The Master said, "They flew away. Mazu then seized the Master by the nose; in his agony, the Master let out a cry of pain.
The Patriarch said, "You say it flies away? At these words, the Master attained realization.

When the Master came for a second audience and stood in attendance, the Patriarch looked at the whisk in the corner of his rope seat. The Master said, "Is this its function, or is it separate from its function?
The Patriarch said, "When you open your mouth in the future, with what will you teach people? The Master picked up the whisk and held it upright. The Patriarch said, "Is this its function?"
Setting aside this matter, the Master intended to hang his whisk back in its original place. The Patriarch let out a thunderous shout, and the Master was left with deafness for three days.
The Master said to the assembly, "The Buddha-dharma is no small matter. In the past, when I was struck by a shout from Great Master Ma, I was likewise left with deafness for three days.

When one's insight is equal to the teacher's, one lacks half the teacher's virtue; only when one's insight surpasses the teacher's does one truly succeed them."
"He is worthy of receiving the transmission. This son possesses a vision that far surpasses his teacher. Baizhang then bowed.
Tongrong said, "Because Huangbo understood the clear function of Mazu’s single shout as cited by Baizhang, he ultimately succeeded Baizhang."

One has attained the vision of Mazu’s great function of spiritual power (*mahā-vīrya*). Yet, one does not yet recognize Mazu himself. If you were to succeed Mazu, your descendants hereafter would lose their true selves.

Although this involves the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) beneath the staff, and one does not see the teacher in the face of immediate circumstances, it nevertheless constitutes the essential dharma for ten thousand ages as a lineage transmission.

It is because of the mind. Furthermore, it clarifies that this gate must necessarily have a lineage of transmission; otherwise, one would indiscriminately fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Zen Master Wenyen of Guangfeng Monastery on Mount Yunmen in Shaozhou, because his own realization was not yet clear, went to study under Muzhou.

This is a definitive judgment. Unless one possesses superior faculties and sharp intelligence, it is impossible even to catch a glimpse of its likeness.
Truly, this is because he has deeply received the "poisonous breath" of Muzhou, and his methods for dealing with people are acridly effective.
Chan Master Shouchu Zonghui of Dongshan in Xiangzhou first went to visit Yunmen. Yunmen asked, "Where have you recently come from? The Master replied, "From Chadu.

In the course of an encounter, it naturally causes people to awaken. Thus, when Yunmen struck him three times with his staff at the beginning, the man’s doubts remained unresolved;

Nowadays, when some possess the functional capacity for such encounters, they only fear that others will not believe them, and so they must repeatedly demonstrate it to others from the very start.

Even if one employs many skillful means, they will merely be like a clear breeze passing by the ear.

There was leakage. Thus, he was able to raise the sun that had already fallen and shake the precious mirror that was about to be buried.

Furthermore, when the tripod legs broke and the sacrificial stew was overturned, I knew then that he was incapable of the task. For this reason—

The *I Ching* says: "The noble person knows the subtle and knows the manifest; he knows the supple and knows the firm. These two masters were such that all men looked up to them.
Chan Master Shandao Xuanjian of Dingzhou was the son of the Zhou family in Jianzhou. He left home at an early age and received full ordination according to his years.

At that time, he was called Zhou Jin’gang (Zhou Vajra). He once said to his fellow students, "A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no loss;

Later, hearing that the Zen seats in the South were flourishing, the Master felt a sense of unease and remarked, "The sons of the renunciant life spend a thousand kalpas studying the Buddha’s deportment and ten thousand kalpas..."

Longtan straightened his body and said, "You have truly arrived at Longtan. The Master remained silent. He then stayed there.

Having received the seal of his mind from Yaoshan, he maintained a bond of spiritual fellowship with Daowu and Yunyan.
Upon leaving Yaoshan, he said to his two companions, "You gentlemen should each occupy a different region and establish the school of Yaoshan; as for me, my nature is by disposition lax."
He lived in the wilds, delighting only in mountains and waters, finding solace in his own emotions and possessing no specialized skills. Later, he learned of my dwelling place;

if he encountered a wise and sharp presiding master (zhuazu), he would send one person to me. Should that person prove capable of being refined, I would transmit to them all that I had acquired throughout my life, thereby repaying the kindness of my former teacher.
Thus, we parted ways and traveled to Huating in Xiuzhou, where we took a small boat and followed [the river].
Because he crossed the river daily to receive those coming and going from the four quarters, people of the time did not know of his lofty conduct;
thus he was called the "Boatman Monk. Later, Daowu arrived at Jingkou and encountered Jiaoshan presiding over the assembly.

Mount said, "The words carry the profound yet there is no path; the tongue speaks yet does not speak. The Master said, "Having fished through the waves of the river, only now is the golden-scaled fish encountered.
Mount then covered his ears. The Master said, "So it is, so it is," and then he instructed him, saying, "Go henceforth."
"You must simply vanish from where you hide your body; do not hide your body where there are no traces.

Instead, go into the deep mountains and, by the side of your spade, seek out one or two others to carry on the lineage so that it never ceases. Thus spoke the Mountain Master.
As he was departing, he looked back again and again. The Master then called out, "Acarya! Shan turned his head.
